item.content:encoded:
Alongside the news that beloved interim skipper Chad Tracy will drop his interim tag, the Boston Red Sox got a slew of positive injury updates. Boston is just six games from the postseason and it needs all the reinforcements it can get.
One of the best, if not the best update is that Willson Contreras is swinging a bat following a scary hit by pitch against the Texas Rangers. Contreras on September 17 took a pitch on the side of his hand, immediately fell to the ground in pain and left the game without delay.
Contreras doesn't easily leave games after being plunked, which has happened 24 times this season. His immediate departure led fans to believe he could've been severely injured. Thankfully, that was not the case, as his imaging came back clean. He believed he fractured his hand because it was numb for a few minutes after the hit, but Contreras avoided the worst.
The Red Sox have not announced an estimated return date for Contreras, but any progress is a good sign. He's been Boston's best hitter all season and leads the team in home runs — the Sox can't afford to go to the postseason without him, especially with the New York Yankees' fearsome rotation ahead in the Wild Card series.
Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela near returns to Red Sox after both take batting practice on September 22
Ceddanne Rafaela also took batting practice on September 22. He hit off Garrett Crochet, who threw 16 pitches before Contreras' turn in the batter's box. The outfielder on September 19 told Alex Speier of The Boston Globe that he hopes to be active for the final homestand of the season, which has already started.
Like Contreras, Rafaela has been one of Boston's most consistent hitters all year. The Soxs offense has faltered without the two in the lineup. If his timeline holds, Rafaela should be back before the postseason so the Red Sox can take full advantage of his clutch timing in huge moments.
Rumors swirl about Curtis Mead's recovery following Garrett Crochet's BP session
There were also rumors that Curtis Mead was expected to hit off Crochet following Rafaela's practice, but there has been no confirmation that he actually swung a bat. The Red Sox acquired Mead from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline to bring a righty power bat to their lineup, but he was plunked in his second Red Sox at-bat and the pitch fractured his wrist.
The most recent update on Mead from mid-September was that he was still feeling soreness in his wrist when he tried to swing. The soreness would need to subside for his hitting progression to start, and given the time of the season, many people assumed his year had reached its end. Given that he may not have hit against Crochet, it might still be.
Red Sox send Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo to Fort Myers to stay loose in case of postseason use
Alongside Crochet, the Red Sox have starters-turned-relievers Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo nearing the end of their respective recoveries. Both pitchers made rehab assignments with the Triple-A Worcester Red Sox before their season ended and they've been sent to Fort Myers to stay loose just in case Boston needs them in the playoffs, according to Chris Cotillo of MassLive.
The Red Sox will have no shortage of pitching depth entering the playoffs, but whether they use any of their rehabbing pitchers is still yet to be seen. Well-rested arms would be helpful, but the team could be concerned about upsetting the chemistry of the preexisting bullpen, which has been one of the best in the sport all year.

item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet reached an important milestone in his road to recovery on Tuesday, facing live hitters on the mound at Fenway Park for the first time since his ill-fated comeback attempt in late May.
Throwing live batting practice against Ceddanne Rafaela, the Red Sox ace threw 16 pitches, one more than originally planned because he spiked a changeup into the dirt on what was supposed to be his final pitch. The left-hander said he was able to ramp up his intensity to a level he hadn’t reached yet, that his fastball was in the 94-96 mph range, and that following the session he got good feedback from Rafaela.
With that crucial box checked, could Crochet’s next time on the mound come in a game setting? Crochet said it’s too soon to say, but he’s cautiously optimistic about his ability to do so.
“You don’t know until you know I suppose. I would say the way that live just went that I could go get outs,” Crochet said. “It depends, obviously, what role they want me in, like I said it’s not really for me to say, I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing is that I felt good out there.”
Crochet has missed the majority of the season due to left shoulder inflammation, which landed him on the injured list in late April after only six starts. What was originally believed to be a short-term injury wound up sidelining Crochet for five months and counting, but after Tuesday’s session there remains a possibility Crochet could factor into the postseason equation for the Red Sox out of the bullpen.
That will be up to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy, Crochet was sure to emphasize.
“This team has had a great year, I think for me to take a spot on the roster then someone would have to lose one, and I would feel bad doing that because this team has pitched their (butts) off the whole season,” Crochet said. “Ultimately that’s going to be something that’s up to the front office and whenever they gauge that I’m ready then I’ll accept that, and in the meantime I’m just going to keep working my butt off.”
Tracy said he was encouraged by Crochet’s outing, noting that his velocity is climbing and the spin on his pitches looked sharp. The next step will be seeing how his body recovers in the upcoming days and mapping out a plan for the weekend.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know,” Tracy said. “I just know that whatever it is it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind.”
Typically the next stage in a throwing progression after throwing live batting practice would be to start a rehab assignment, but given that the minor league season ended this past weekend, that isn’t an option for Crochet. Time also isn’t on the left-hander’s side, so if Crochet is going to pitch in a game before the playoffs, he would have to be activated at some point over the final homestand.
Tracy said those are all factors the club is considering, and while he believes Crochet would be up for the challenge of jumping right into a playoff series, they have to be realistic about where he’s at when it comes time to decide who will be on the playoff roster.
“Knowing the player, if he was healthy and we felt he could he’d probably be like ‘I’m not going to be afraid of that,'” Tracy said. “That being said, we have to consider it and just be very mindful of what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us, really? Understanding you don’t want to leave yourself short, so for me it’s been step by step, the next step would be sometime this weekend, let’s see what that entails, and we’ll go from there.”
Rafaela, Contreras getting close
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) remain sidelined with their respective injuries, but Tracy said both are getting close to a return.
“(Rafaela) is doing much better, we’re getting close there, and Willson’s also doing much better, he was able to swing pretty aggressively in the cage again today,” Tracy said, adding that Rafaela was scheduled to run and Contreras was set to take batting practice on the field. “(We’ll) let them get through their whole day, see where they’re at and assess, but I think we’re getting pretty close with both of them.”
Staying ready
With the minor league season finished the Red Sox have sent a contingent of players who may potentially factor into the club’s plans the rest of the way to Fort Myers so they can stay ready in the event they’re needed.
Tracy did not have the full list of players available when asked Tuesday, but some of those headed to Fort Myers include pitchers Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Jedixson Paez, Tyler Samaniego and Wyatt Olds, infielders Romy Gonzalez, Franklin Arias and Tsung-Che Cheng, and outfielder Braiden Ward.
Veteran catcher Tomas Nido has also come up from Worcester to serve as an extra catcher on the taxi squad for the Red Sox.
Extra innings
The Red Sox announced Eli White underwent successful Lisfranc repair surgery on his right foot Tuesday. The procedure was performed by Dr. Martin O’Malley at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. … Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) is feeling much better but is still a day or two away from a return to the mound. … Curtis Mead (fractured left wrist) has resumed swinging a regular bat and is taking overhand batting practice, but while the Red Sox haven’t ruled out a possible return, Tracy acknowledged that time isn’t on his side.

item.content:encoded:
Once again, Garrett Crochet donned a full Red Sox uniform, made the walk from the bullpen to the mound, and pitched at Fenway Park on Tuesday afternoon. This time, he faced a live hitter -- in the form of Ceddanne Rafaela -- as he took another step toward returning to the mound for Boston.
And for the first time in what's been a long recovery period, the 27-year-old said he feels ready to contribute.
"I would say, the way that that live [batting practice] just went, that I could go get outs," Crochet told reporters inside the Red Sox clubhouse.
That being said, Crochet shared that he has some hesitance to joining the roster, though it has nothing to do with his own health.
"This team's had a great year. I think that for me to take a spot on the roster, then someone would have to lose one. And I would feel bad doing that, because this team has pitched their ass off the whole season," Crochet said. "Ultimately, that's something that's gonna be up to the front office. And whenever they gauge that I'm ready, then I'll accept that. In the meantime, I'm just gonna keep working my butt off."
More Red Sox Coverage
Crochet's work on Tuesday involved 16 pitches, and he estimated he was sitting at 94-96 mph on his fastball velocity. The left-hander said how well he recovers on Wednesday will be a significant determinant on his ability to pitch in games. Yet when asked if he'll pitch in a regular-season game this weekend or save his return for the postseason, he is leaving that decision to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy.
"I think that I'm just gonna do whatever they tell me to do, to be honest," he said. "I think that [live BPs] and games, obviously it's a big step up and the pressure of the moment, I suppose, and the intensity. But I don't think that there's a set amount of [live BPs] that need to be thrown before a game."
Tracy, who officially dropped the interim tag earlier in the day, said that whatever decision is made on Crochet, it will be "done with Garrett's best interests in mind."
"Looking at what is he able to accomplish this week, and what does the playoffs require?" Tracy explained. "And then deciding can he fit that role or not based on what he's done."
Ceddanne Rafaela
Rafaela, who hasn't played since Sept. 2 due to a hamstring injury, partook in the live BP with Crochet as he nears a return to the lineup.
"Much better," Tracy said on Rafaela. "Getting close there."
Rafaela has produced the best offensive season of his career, as he's batted .282 with a .760 OPS in 135 games, while continuing to provide Gold Glove-level defense in center field.
Willson Contreras
Tracy also shared a positive injury update on Willson Contreras, who continues to improve after taking a pitch off his right hand last Thursday.
Tracy said that Contreras is "doing much better" and is "swinging aggressively" as he works his way back to full strength.
Aroldis Chapman
Closer Aroldis Chapman hasn't pitched since Sept. 13 due to some lat tightness, but Tracy had yet another positive injury update.
"He's getting very close," Tracy said. "I think we're a day or two away from him being ready to roll."
Group staying ready in Fort Myers
The Red Sox are keeping a team of reinforcements ready in Fort Myers for the playoff run, in case anybody is needed as an injury replacement along the way. That list of players includes:
- SP Tanner Houck
- SP Johan Oviedo
- SS/2B Franklin Arias
- OF Braiden Ward
- RP Wyatt Olds
- SS/2B Tsung-Che Cheng
- RP Tyler Samaniego
- 1B/2B Romy Gonzalez
- RP Jedixson Paez
Curtis Mead
Perhaps the lone negative injury update from Tracy was on second baseman Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist in his first game with the Red Sox on July 27.
"Haven't ruled it out yet. It's gonna be tough," Tracy said when asked if Mead might be able to return for the first round of the playoffs.
Tracy said that Mead is taking some overhand batting practice, but there may not be enough time for Mead to progress to being game-ready.
"I said we would probably be a little aggressive to see how the hand responds," Tracy said. "Have not ruled it out. It's just we're getting up against it a bit."

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why. Justin Slaten had quietly turned into one of the more trustworthy arms in this bullpen, working to a 2.84 ERA over his final two months of availability before elbow trouble sidelined him in August.
Now we know the full picture: an evaluation revealed degenerative changes in the flexor mass of his right elbow, and rather than push for a return with the postseason approaching, the Red Sox are having him get a PRP injection and start planning for 2027 instead.
On the year, he had thirty-six appearances, a 4.60 ERA overall, but provided a real chunk of high-leverage relief work, which is now gone for the stretch run. That's a real hole, absolutely. It's also not the whole story right now, and it's worth taking a breath before assuming the bullpen just got worse.
Garrett Crochet was the AL Cy Young runner-up last season, an 18-5, 2.59 ERA workhorse who threw 205.1 innings and struck out 255 batters. What a lot of people forget is that before all of that, Crochet broke into pro ball as a reliever with the Chicago White Sox, sitting comfortably in the upper 90s and regularly touching triple digits in short bursts. That's exactly the version the Red Sox may get back down the stretch.
He hasn't pitched in a game since throwing six scoreless innings on April 25, and after months sidelined with a shoulder issue that turned into more of a lingering problem, he just threw his first bullpen sessions in nearly three months. There isn't time left to stretch him back out as a starter, but a Crochet who can air it out for one to three innings at a time is exactly the profile that's thrived in October before.
Pair that with a Payton Tolle start going five or six innings, Crochet bridging the seventh and eighth, and Aroldis Chapman closing it out, and that's a real, dangerous alignment behind Sonny Gray in a Game 1.
Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo are trending toward returns to Red Sox bullpen alongside Garrett Crochet
Crochet isn't walking through that door alone, either. Tanner Houck is further along than anyone, working back from UCL surgery and already up to three innings and 48 pitches in a rehab outing for Double-A Portland, allowing just one run with four strikeouts, before moving on to Triple-A Worcester to keep building and facing some better competition.
Johan Oviedo, who Boston acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates over the winter, finally made his own rehab appearance with Worcester this week after missing more than five months with a flexor strain, which is a sign he could factor into the bullpen picture before the year is out. Kutter Crawford is the longer shot of the group, hasn't pitched for the big club since 2024, and there are only unconfirmed "rumblings" he could get a look at Worcester this week. Even if that goes nowhere in 2026, he's still under team control for two more seasons.
Losing Slaten hurts, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But between Crochet, Houck, and Oviedo all trending in the right direction at the same time, Boston may be walking into the stretch run with more usable, high-upside arms than it's had healthy at any single point all season.

The Boston Red Sox acquired Johan Oviedo from the Pittsburgh Pirates in the winter, thinking he would be their No. 5 starter.
However, Connelly Early won that job in spring training, and Oviedo was relegated to the bullpen. Near the end of spring training, his velocity was noticeably down, and he gave up six hits and four earned runs in his only outing for the Red Sox this year. He was placed on the injured list with an elbow sprain and pitched in a rehab game with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday.
His velocity was back up, topping out at 98.5 mph and averaging 95.9 mph with his fastball. That is where the Red Sox expected him to be when they got him. The Red Sox could use a starter right now, but just like Garrett Crochet, there is not time to get Oviedo built up as a starter.
"You always have great dreams about playing for a team like (Boston) with a lot of history," Oviedo said, per MassLive's Katie Morrison-O'Day. "You want to fill up your spot, and not being available to help the team from the beginning definitely has been a challenge for me. If I still have a shot to help the team in any way, in the last few weeks of the season or the playoffs, I'm just trying to be ready."
"I'm more than open to fill any role, and not finish the season on the IL," Oviedo added. "It's definitely not the plan for any pitcher. But all I'm trying to do right now is be healthy and be available for the team if they need me.
Oviedo pitched 2 1/3 innings on Thursday, notching four strikeouts. He gave up one run, two hits and a walk, landing 20 of his 30 pitches for strikes. He threw his four-seamer, slider, sinker, curveball and changeup in the outing.
Oviedo is a talented pitcher, and it's very possible that he would have been a staple in the rotation this year had he not gotten hurt. The minor league season is about to end, so there won't be many more opportunities for him to get rehab outings. He is unsure if he will be on the taxi squad or get to pitch for the Red Sox this year. However, he wants to be ready if his number is called.
"I've been on a playoff roster before but never pitched," Oviedo said. "So it's definitely one of the dreams that I want to accomplish. If Boston will give me that chance, if the team needs me, hopefully I can be ready for it."

item.content:encoded:
WORCESTER -- Johan Oviedo is racing against the clock to get back and help the Red Sox.
Making his first rehab start since hitting the injured list on April 3 with a flexor sprain in his right elbow, Oviedo topped out at 98.5 mph with his sinker and went 2 1/3 innings.
The righty allowed one run on two hits and a walk, striking out four. The three swings and misses he recorded came on his four-seamer.
He was efficient, using 30 pitches to reach the third inning.
“(I was) super excited to get the first one out,” Oviedo said. “I just feel blessed, and hopefully I can continue to get healthy.”
Oviedo averaged just under 96 mph with both his four-seamer and his sinker, but said he wasn’t worried about what the radar was reading.
“Velo has never really been a concern,” Oviedo said. “It’s more about health-wise, how the arm feels. It’s more about making sure that my body moves well. If the body’s moving well, I know the velo will be there. But I mean, it’s always a good sign to see good velo on the radar.”
Oviedo was acquired by the Red Sox in December in a five-player deal that sent Jhostynxon Garcia to the Pirates. He only got to make one appearance before landing on the injured list in April.
“You always have great dreams about playing for a team like (Boston) with a lot of history,” Oviedo said. “You want to fill up your spot, and not being available to help the team from the beginning definitely has been a challenge for me. If I still have a shot to help the team in any way, in the last few weeks of the season or the playoffs, I’m just trying to be ready.”
Primarily a starter throughout his career, it’s possible Oviedo may not have enough time to stretch out as a starter before the Red Sox need him, and he says he’s open to however the team could use him.
“I’m more than open to fill any role, and not finish the season on the IL,” Oviedo said. “It’s definitely not the plan for any pitcher. But all I’m trying to do right now is be healthy and be available for the team if they need me.
Oviedo is no stranger to rehabbing; he missed all of 2024 after undergoing Tommy John surgery but returned to make nine starts with a 3.57 ERA in 2025.
“(There were) definitely a lot of feelings,” Oviedo said about making his first appearance in a game in months. “But as a professional, you’re trying to keep everything under control, put your feelings in balance. In the past, on the first outing, you [might] try to do more than what you can do. So today I was trying to keep it the same, treat it like another live BP in Florida.”
Oviedo is running out of days to pitch in games as he tries to get back to the major-league team, as the WooSox’ season ends on Sunday and the opportunity for in-game rehab outings ends with it. The pitcher said he wasn’t aware of what the plan was going forward and whether he’d be part of the Red Sox’ taxi squad.
With nine games left in the Red Sox’ season, there’s a chance the next time Oviedo is with the team is in the postseason,
“I’ve been on a playoff roster before but never pitched,” Oviedo said. “So it’s definitely one of the dreams that I want to accomplish. If Boston will give me that chance, if the team needs me, hopefully I can be ready for it.”
Notes
- Braiden Ward, who has been a topic of conversation since Red Sox manager Chad Tracy brought up his name as a potential late-season call-up, stole his 60th base of the season on Wednesday. Ward leads the International League in stolen bases and holds the WooSox record in steals. He’s 60-for-69 (87%) on attempts this season.
“Speed kills, and it never slumps,” WooSox manager Iggy Suarez said. “Any time you have speed like that, it can change the game; it can be a pain.”
- Tanner Houck is set to pitch for the WooSox again on Saturday after striking out the side in an inning of work on Tuesday for Worcester.
Performance of the Week
As the season winds down for Worcester, Allan Castro is heating up. The outfielder has bashed five home runs in 15 games this month, including two multi-home-run games over the last week. Castro’s two home runs and four RBI propelled the WooSox to a come-from-behind win on Wednesday.
Castro’s hot streak boosts his season slash line to .251/.325/.387 with 16 doubles, 14 home runs, and a triple.
What’s Next
The 2026 season wraps up over the weekend with three final games against the Durham Bulls. Sunday will feature a pre-game meet-the-team autograph party.
The WooSox aren’t officially eliminated from postseason contention, but need a whole lot to go right for them to clinch over the three teams currently above them in the standings with three games to go.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.

The Boston Red Sox starter is working his way back from a right elbow injury.
Video Transcript
What's up, everyone?
Zach Coe here for Roundtable.
Ahead of Tuesday night's loss to the Rangers, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters that reliever Justin Slayton's season was over after an orthopedic visit revealed degenerative changes in his flexor mass, which required a PRP injection, effectively ending his season.
So obviously, the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in baseball, backend of Aroldis Chapman, Justin Slayton, and Tayron Guerrero when he returns from the injured list.
But the loss of Slayton is still a really big one for this Red Sox bullpen, especially in the postseason when managers tend to be more aggressive with the hooks on both starters and relievers.
It was a pretty underwhelming season for Slayton when you look at the final line.
It was a 4.60 ERA in 31 1/3 innings.
But he was prone to a couple blowup starts, and that really inflated his ERA for much of the season.
It'll be interesting to see how Tracy's able to piece together the bullpen in Slayton's absence.
Of course, like I said, you have the backend pretty solidified with Tayron Guerrero handling the seventh, Garrett Whitlock in the eighth to All-Star Aroldis Chapman, who's been one of the best closers in baseball over the last two seasons.
But it's how you get to them that I really have some concerns about, and there are plenty of guys that are available to fill that role, but it's whether or not they'll be able to capitalize on their opportunities.
First one being Greg Weiser.
I wrote about it a little bit earlier, but ever since he was recalled from his brief demotion to Triple-A, he's been incredible for the Red Sox, stepping up as they lost guys like Whitlock to an IL stint, Slayton, who landed on the IL shortly after Whitlock, and most recently Guerrero.
There's also Tanner Houk, who's working his way back from Tommy John surgery he underwent last year.
He's gonna try to make a return in a bullpen capacity for the last week of the season.
And then there's the big wild card of it all in Garrett Crochet, who continues to throw side sessions as he tries to get back in a relief role for the postseason.
He's been on the injured list since April 29th with left shoulder inflammation.
So any of those guys are more than capable of stepping up and filling that role.
It's just gonna be about whether or not they're, one, healthy enough to go out there and throw on a near nightly basis like the team might need them to in the postseason, and two, whether or not they're gonna be productive enough.
Obviously, with Houk, he's coming back from Tommy John surgery, and typically you see guys be a little bit wild with their control when they first come back from Tommy John.
We saw it in Houk's first relea-- We saw it in his first rehab appearance with Portland.
He walked two guys, and a run scored as a result.
But it's been a little bit better, since then in the two appearances following that.
So we'll see if that is something that he can shake.
And then Crochet, he's just We haven't seen him in so long, it's tough to say whether or not he's gonna be as effective as he once was.
And even if he isn't able to get to the 2025 Cy Young runner-up caliber, can he at least give you enough to kind of bridge that gap between the starter and to the backend of your bullpen?
And then there's kind of a wild card in it all, and a bit of a forgotten man in Johan Oviedo, who obviously has electric stuff, but he's made only one appearance in a Red Sox uniform before landing on the IL with right elbow inflammation.
So he's planning on making a rehab appearance with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday night, and then they'll figure out the next steps with him.
But Red Sox have plenty of options to fill that void left behind by Slayton.

Originally viewed as one of the favorites to start the season in the Opening Day rotation, Red Sox right-hander Johan Oviedo wound up making just one appearance out of the bullpen before going on the shelf with a right elbow strain.
Now after missing nearly the entire season, Oviedo may finally be nearing a return.
Oviedo began a rehab assignment at Triple-A Worcester on Thursday, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in his first game action since late March.
The 28-year-old threw 30 pitches, 20 for strikes, while allowing one run on two hits and a walk while striking out four. Oviedo allowed an RBI double with one out in the top of the second before striking out the final three batters he faced.
More encouragingly, Oviedo’s fastball averaged 95.9 mph and topped out at 98.5, a sizable jump from the 92-93 he averaged earlier in the season.
Originally acquired last winter from the Pittsburgh Pirates as part of the Jhostynxon Garcia trade, Oviedo was initially expected to provide rotation depth as a possible high-ceiling power arm. Oviedo had previously missed extensive time due to Tommy John surgery, but finished his last season in Pittsburgh strong with a 3.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts over nine starts down the stretch.
The righty entered spring as one of the favorites for the No. 5 rotation spot, but after some promising early starts began showing signs of wear. The last rotation spot wound up going to Connelly Early, with Oviedo making the team as a reliever, and he made one appearance against the Houston Astros on March 30, allowing four runs over 3 2/3 innings.
Oviedo has been on the injured list ever since, but now he could be a dark horse candidate for the Red Sox playoff roster along with Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet, who are also working their way back from extended injury absences.
Upcoming starters
Ranger Suarez will start Friday’s series opener against the Tampa Bay Rays, but the Red Sox’s other starters remain to be determined. Payton Tolle would normally be in line to start Saturday but Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas on Thursday that the club is still deciding how it wants to handle the weekend.
Brayan Bello, who was limited to 19 pitches over 1 2/3 innings on Tuesday, would presumably be a candidate to start one of this weekend’s games.

The Boston Red Sox made one of the very best moves in baseball for the 2026 season, despite the fact that some fans didn't initially believe in the deal.
While searching for a No. 2 starter last offseason, Boston turned to the St. Louis Cardinals and swung a deal for three-time All-Star Sonny Gray. With the Red Sox searching for another elite starter, some wondered if Gray was better suited for a mid-to-back of the rotation spot, rather than the No. 2 spot for a club with World Series aspirations. He has more than delivered and has been Boston's best starter all season. Gray's going to get Cy Young Award votes and Boston should do what it can to try to keep him in town beyond the 2026 season. If he plays, he'll cost a pretty penny. MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that some in the industry believe Gray will get a deal in the range of three years and $75 million — or more — if he continues his career.
"As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago," Cotillo wrote. "Interestingly, though, Gray has not committed to pitching again in 2027. In a recent interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said he would retire 'in a heartbeat' if his family signaled that he was wanted back home year-round, even if that meant retiring after the end of this year."
The Red Sox Should Do Everything To Keep Sonny Gray
That's actually also the same deal that the Cardinals gave Gray before the 2024 season as well. He inked a three-year, $75 million pact that he's currently in the final year of. After the season, Gray has a $30 million mutual option for the 2027 season with a $10 million buyout. If Boston picks up its end of the buyout and Gray opts out, then the buyout would be forfeited.
Gray has pitched well enough in a Red Sox uniform to get paid again — if he keeps pitching. So far this season, he has a 17-5 record, 2.76 ERA and 4.0 wins above replacement in 156 2/3 innings pitched. When it comes to Gray, his age stands out at 36 years old. But it hasn't stopped him yet. The price of pitching has gone up in a big way. A deal with a $25 million annual value, as Cotillo pointed out, would be in the range of guys like Michael King, Sean Manaea, and Eovaldi. It would be just above guys like Aaron Nola, Seth Lugo, Robbie Ray and Luis Severino. Gray has been better than all of these guys so far this season.
When it comes to the Red Sox, there isn't as much pitching depth down in the minors as there once was. Over the last year, Boston has traded guys like Hunter Dobbins, Richard Fitts, Brandon Clarke, Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, among others. Plus, Connelly Early was traded as well.
Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, and Jake Bennett are locks for the 2027 rotation. Johan Oviedo is someone who could play a role. Tanner Houck is another guy who could as well. We've seen all season how impactful injuries are to the rotation. You never have enough arms. A dependable veteran like Gray for the next few years should be a necessity. It's no guarantee that he pitches beyond the 2026 season, but if he does, it should be in a Boston uniform.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now.
For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs.
The last two games have been more of a struggle for Miller, though. In 1.1 innings, he’s given up four runs. That includes three runs in Wednesday’s rough loss to the Texas Rangers, which was good enough for Miller to earn a loss.
Boston Red Sox RP Erik Miller Opened Up on Struggles
Following Wednesday’s loss, Erik Miller faced the media following the game. There, he explained that his main issue on Wednesday was that he had control issues. Those control issues put him in bad counts, which made him predictable.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well,” Erik Miller said. “Just not getting ahead of guys. Getting behind. Falling into hitters’ counts… Guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end well. Just kind of working through some stuff right now.”
Red Sox fans and media both noticed Miller saying that he’s working through some stuff. Luckily, that doesn’t mean an injury. It’s more a reference to letting his mechanics get away from him.
“Yeah. Some stuff I’m trying to clean up a little. At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. You’ve been doing really well and some bad habits kind of come up. So, I’ve just got to work through it. Get back to what I was doing and go from there,” Miller said.
The Red Sox need the version of Miller they’ve largely gotten since the trade. He has a 2.87 ERA in Boston, to go along with a 1.277 WHIP and 14.9 strikeouts per nine. That’s in 15.2 innings over 16 appearances.
Garrett Crochet Will Return to the Red Sox as a Reliever
The Red Sox bullpen is set to get a major boost soon. Ace pitcher Garrett Crochet is getting ready to make his return, but it won’t be as a starter. It’ll be as another power lefty for the bullpen to use.
The expectation had been that Crochet won’t be able to make a rehab and would jump back in right as the first-round of the playoffs start. That may not be the case now. It was recently reported that he could be ready even sooner. That means he’ll potentially pitch in the regular season as a kind of rehab.
“The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason,” Chris Cotillo of MassLive wrote. “It’s not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what’s effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings.”
It’s excellent news for the Red Sox. With Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, a healthy Garrett Crochet, and Erik Miller, Boston can feel very confident if they get just five innings from a starter.

item.content:encoded:
For the last two seasons, Garrett Whitlock has been one of the best pitchers the Boston Red Sox's bullpen has to offer. But the righty has considered changing that.
Whitlock told Tim Healey of The Boston Globe that he would consider a return to life as a starting pitcher (subscription required). Whitlock in 2021 debuted with Boston as a reliever, but he began starting some games shortly after in 2022. He made four starts in 2024 and planned to take his full season as a starter, but a UCL injury derailed that plan.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to," Whitlock said, via Healey. "So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Some fans and people in the Red Sox organization could be excited to hear Whitlock say he's interested in reprising his role as a starting pitcher. Boston has just one righty starter in its rotation this year, Sonny Gray, and he'll be a free agent at the end of the season, barring an unexpected contract extension. Whitlock's success in the bullpen could translate to more in the rotation and he could compete for Gray's former spot.
Red Sox should keep Garrett Whitlock in bullpen despite his willingness to return to a starting role
But Whitlock's history as a starter isn't as clean as it is from the bullpen. Whitlock went on the injured list twice in the 2022-23 seasons with hip and elbow issues. He missed all but four appearances of the 2024 season after he underwent the internal brace procedure to repair his UCL. His elbow even flared up after a period of heavy use out of the bullpen this season. Adding starts into his repertoire hasn't worked before, and though it could work now since Whitlock said he's more in-tune with his body, it isn't a risk the Sox should be willing to take.
Whitlock has had more success as a reliever than as a starter, though he's pitched far more in relief and the sample sizes are far from equal. The veteran has posted a 4.29 ERA over 109 innings across 23 appearances as a starter and a 2.37 ERA over 254.1 frames in relief. The Red Sox need right-handed rotation depth, but they also have Tanner Houck, Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo recovering from injury, and none of them have established themselves in another role as seamlessly as Whitlock has.
Whitock told Healey that he would return to a starting role if the Red Sox want him to (he's under team control until after the 2028 season due to two club options) or if any new team he signs with wants him to change. For now and in 2027, the Red Sox should stick with the good thing they have, which is Whitlock as one of the most dangerous relievers in the league.

The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though.
It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing.
"The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason," Cotillo wrote. "It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.

Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

The Boston Red Sox could have a slew of pitching reinforcements returning before the playoffs begin, including Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, and maybe even Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Justin Slaten will not be among them.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on September 15 told reporters (including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe) that Slaten got a PRP injection in his arm to address a flexor issue. His season is over after multiple attempts to ramp up for a rehab assignment and eventual return.
Slaten has been quite injury prone over his three years with the Red Sox. He went on the injured list for the first time this season in early April and didn't return until mid-May. For the second straight year, he'll finish his season with less than 35 innings pitched.
Justin Slaten's season with Red Sox ends after he gets PCP injection for flexor injury
The righty has dabbled in the extremes this season, finishing with a 4.60 ERA over 31.1 innings. In June, Slaten's worst month this year, he allowed nine runs on 17 hits over 11 outings. July was his best, during which he let up just one run on five hits over nine appearances. His WHIP has starkly increased over the past year, from 1.09 in 2025 to 1.37.
When the Red Sox can get Slaten's best, he's one of the biggest threats out of their bullpen. But he's often injured or prone to blowups that keep him from showing the best he can offer. It will be interesting to see his role next season when Boston has more healthy pitching depth it could push to the bullpen.
Red Sox confirm Kristian Campbell's season is over due to foot injury, ending breakout
Kristian Campbell's season has also ended prematurely due to an injury. The outfielder will be out for the rest of the year due to a left foot contusion, according to Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
The WooSox pulled Campbell from their September 8 game due to the injury. Even before the announcement of his IL stint, it was evident that Campbell's season could be over, as Worcester's last regular season game is on Septembet 20.
Campbell's injury ends a resurgent second half for the 24 year old. He slashed .311/.430/.497 over 51 games after the All-Star break and, had he been healthy, he might've been selected to come up and help the major league team while Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White are injured.
Romy Gonzalez continues tear following arm injury scare with WooSox
On the same day Campbell was pulled from the WooSox's lineup, Romy Gonzalez was, too. An arm injury led to a week on the shelf for the utility infielder, but he joined the Triple-A lineup again on September 15.
Gonzalez has resumed the tear he was on before his arm flared up. He logged two hits, including a double, in his return and boosted his September slash line to .500/.520/.727 over six games. Gonzalez has hit so well lately that it could be time to call him back up to the major leagues to give Boston's slumping offense a boost.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.
